Creating a separate administration

The formation of Gujarat involved more than drawing a new boundary. A single state administration had to be divided into two functioning state administrations without interrupting public services. The new state required its own government departments, administrative offices, legislative institutions, High Court, public services and financial arrangements.

The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, therefore contained detailed provisions for distributing the former Bombay State's assets and liabilities, allocating government employees, continuing public utilities and reorganising state corporations.

Division of assets and financial resources

The Act did not distribute every asset and liability using one common formula. Different rules applied according to the nature and location of the property or obligation.

AreaArrangement under the Act
Land and goodsGenerally passed to the state in whose territory the property or goods were located.
Treasury and bank balancesDivided according to the specified population ratio of Maharashtra and Gujarat.
Loans and public debtAllocated using rules based on the purpose of the loan, the beneficiary, territorial location or capital expenditure.
Pensions and provident fundsPension liabilities attributable to service before division were shared in the population ratio; provident fund liability for employees serving on the appointed day followed their permanent state allotment.
Contracts and state undertakingsUndertakings followed their location; contracts exclusively serving one state passed to it, while other contracts initially passed to Maharashtra, subject to financial adjustment by agreement or Central Government order.

The Act defined the population ratio of Maharashtra and Gujarat as 66.31:33.69, respectively. This ratio was used for the division of treasury and bank balances and specified common funds. It was not a universal rule for dividing every asset, debt or liability.

Capital construction provision

Section 51 provided for the transfer of securities worth ₹10 crore from the former Bombay State's cash-balance investment account to Gujarat in connection with the construction of its capital. The Act also provided for a Special Revenue Reserve Fund in Gujarat.

Continuity of employees and public services

The division of the state also required the allocation of personnel belonging to the All-India Services and other government services. The Act provided for the Central Government to determine their allocation to the successor states by order. It also allowed officers to continue in the same posts initially, preventing an immediate breakdown in government administration.

Electricity and water supply required particular attention because the generating stations, distribution installations, reservoirs and catchment areas did not necessarily fall within the same state after reorganisation.

The Act therefore allowed the Central Government to issue directions to maintain existing electricity and water supply arrangements where territorial changes might otherwise disadvantage an area. The Bombay State Electricity Board and State Warehousing Corporation were also allowed to continue functioning temporarily. They were to cease functioning on 1 October 1960 or an earlier date specified by the Central Government, after which their assets, rights and liabilities could be apportioned.

Ahmedabad and the development of Gandhinagar

Ahmedabad served as the capital of Gujarat from 1960 to 1970. Establishing a separate state required a planned capital with suitable government offices and administrative infrastructure.

The city of Gandhinagar was established on 2 August 1965 as the new capital. Its development was intended to reduce the population pressure on Ahmedabad and provide a planned administrative centre. However, the capital was shifted from Ahmedabad to Gandhinagar only in 1970. Therefore, the establishment of Gandhinagar in 1965 and the transfer of the capital in 1970 are two different events.

Early economic and developmental priorities

The newly formed state also needed to expand its agricultural, industrial and public infrastructure. A retrospective account published in Yojana in May 2021 by the then Chief Minister of Gujarat identified several development needs at the time of state formation:

  • Improving irrigation facilities through adequate water and electricity supply.
  • Developing a better road network and transport infrastructure.
  • Establishing government offices and infrastructure for efficient administration.
  • Expanding technology and industrial facilities.
  • Developing educational institutions and healthcare facilities.
  • Strengthening agriculture and animal husbandry programmes.

These points describe development priorities recalled in a later account; they should not be treated as a contemporaneous statistical inventory of every facility available in 1960.

Prelims focus

  • The population ratio specified in the Bombay Reorganisation Act was 66.31:33.69 for Maharashtra and Gujarat.
  • Gujarat received securities worth ₹10 crore for construction of its capital.
  • Ahmedabad remained the capital of Gujarat from 1960 to 1970.
  • Gandhinagar was established on 2 August 1965; the capital shifted there in 1970.
  • The Act provided for the allocation of employees, assets, liabilities and public-service institutions.
  • Electricity and water supply arrangements were protected to avoid disruption after reorganisation.
  • Trap: The population ratio was not the universal formula for dividing every asset and liability.

[Sources: The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, sections 2(f), 45–54, 68–70 and 80–84, India Code (consulted 22 November 2026); Ahmedabad District, Government of Gujarat, History; Gandhinagar District, Government of Gujarat, History (consulted 22 November 2026); Yojana, May 2021, Growth Story of Gujarat, p. 13 (consulted 22 November 2026).]
